doc.title: Jackie Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: First gigs and dances in the fifties
summary: He cannot pinpoint his first professional job; he played neighborhood dances, where good time mattered, with Lindy, mambo and calypso crowds.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: When was your first like professional gig?

A gig? Gee I can’t, it’s hard to really pinpoint my first professional job although I know I played, I had a set of drums and I was playing and people would call, they knew I could play drums, so they would call around, you know the different people in the neighborhood that had dances or something like that. They would call. They would call me and say well hey man I got a gig or something like that. A dance. There were a lot of dances and stuff then, you know, which was beautiful. So I did a lot of those things. But I couldn’t really pinpoint the first time I played a — it’s hard for me to really pinpoint.

The dance thing comes up over and over and over, connected with jazz, you know that it is and was a dance music. And from a drummer’s standpoint, I would imagine that you had to really pay attention to what worked with the dancers.

Oh, certainly, sure, sure. In the first place, the most important thing was to have good time. You have to have good time because they’ll let you know. They’ll say well what’s going on up there with this band. They’re the first ones to let you know, the dancers, you know, good dancers.
